artifacts.body:
## The business

Cedar Valley Selections Inc. runs a pita chip manufacturing facility in Oldcastle, roughly the Muncie area, and describes its own work — in its own grant listing — as scaling up automation, adding quality assurance and food-safety steps, and improving "map processing" to lift efficiency, quality and production capacity [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description]. That phrasing, plus a $75,000 Industrial Research Assistance Program award in 2023 for "Scale-Up Process and Implementation of Automation" [block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[1]] and a further $30,000 youth employment award in 2025 [block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[0]], places this squarely as a food processor mid-way through modernizing a physical production line — dough or base product through baking/frying, seasoning, packing, and out the door — with federal support behind that transition. No headcount is recorded and no equipment list survives in the record [what the grant funded: not recorded], so where exactly the automation landed on the floor is a gap, not a fact.

## Findings

1. The company has taken two federal automation awards three years apart rather than one — $75,000 in 2023 named specifically for scale-up and automation implementation, and $30,000 in 2025 for a youth hire [block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[1], block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[0]] — which suggests the first project did not finish the job of removing manual work from the plant, since they went back for more support rather than declaring it done. What was actually bought with either award is not recorded, which is a discovery question, not something to assume.

2. The evidence shows a named decision maker who is the direct contact, with no headcount on file [block7_people.flags.named_decision_maker, block7_people.contact_tier] — that reads as an owner-run shop where quoting, order intake and production paperwork most likely still sit with the owner or a small handful of staff rather than dedicated departments, which is exactly the size where one workflow removed by hand is felt immediately.

3. If the quoting desk is turning out somewhere between 40 and 150 quotes a month at 45 to 180 minutes of manual work each, done by someone paid $22 to $34 an hour and loaded at the U.S. manufacturing benefits multiplier of 1.496 times wages [BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation], that manual quoting load alone could be costing the plant anywhere from about $12,000 a year on the light case to well over $270,000 on the busy one — a wide span precisely because none of those inputs is confirmed yet.

4. Against the eleven-company food and beverage peer group, Cedar Valley sits behind on capital deployed — about $150,000 counting the matching money required, with 7 of 11 peers ahead of them — which reads as an industry pattern of larger single investments among peers rather than evidence this particular plant is under-resourced.

## Three approaches

### 1. Quote Assembler

Draft a new quote from a past job's materials and pricing instead of building it from scratch.

What gets built is a quote assembler that drafts a new price quote from a past job's materials and pricing rather than starting from a blank sheet — for a plant selling into grocery, food-service or private-label accounts, that connects to whatever spreadsheet or order log currently holds job history, since no ordering platform is confirmed in the file. On the target reading, if the desk turns out somewhere between 77 and 113 quotes a month at 90 to 135 minutes each, done by someone at $22 to $34 an hour loaded at 1.496 times wages [BLS], and the build removes 37 to 43 percent of that effort, the hours handed back are worth roughly $16,700 to $67,400 a year against a $600-to-$2,500 build, paying back inside the first one to two months. Observed: the grant record shows this company has already run one federally funded automation project and returned for a second award, which reads as a shop already comfortable buying outside technical help. Assumed, verify on the call: the actual quote volume, minutes per quote, wage, and which system — if any — currently holds job history and pricing; the tech-stack evidence on file resolves to an unrelated company's website and cannot be trusted for this plant's own software.

1-2 weeks · $600-$2,500 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the target reading, returns $16,653-$67,445 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 1-2 months

### 2. Machine Utilization & Scrap Report

Turn data the machines already record into a weekly utilization and scrap read.

What gets built is a weekly utilization-and-scrap report pulled from whatever the machines already record, so the owner sees line downtime and waste as a number instead of a impression. The grant record itself names "quality assurance / food safety implementations" and "map processing" as funded scope [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description], which is a real observed signal that some production-tracking capability already exists on the floor to build from — what form it takes is not recorded. On the target reading, if the plant runs somewhere between 247 and 373 machine-shifts a month, each carrying 14 to 19 minutes of manual reporting work, done at $22 to $34 an hour loaded at 1.496 times wages [BLS], and a report removes 53 to 62 percent of that effort, the hours saved are worth roughly $11,800 to $45,300 a year against a $2,500-to-$8,000 diagnostic. Observed: the funded scope names quality and process work directly. Assumed, verify on the call: how many machine-shifts actually run a month, whether data is captured in a PLC, a paper log or a spreadsheet, and what "map processing" from the grant title actually refers to on the floor.

1-2 weeks · $2,500-$8,000 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the target reading, returns $11,834-$45,278 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 1-9 months

### 3. Enquiry Front Door

Answer, capture and route an inbound enquiry within the hour it lands.

What gets built is a front door: something that answers an inbound enquiry — a broker asking for lead times, a retail account asking about specs — captures it and routes it within the hour rather than whenever a shared inbox gets checked. It would connect to whatever contact form or inbox handles that mail today; the site evidence on file describes an unrelated healthcare-payments company, not this plant, so it cannot be assumed to describe Cedar Valley's actual front door. On the aggressive reading, if 27 to 43 enquiries a month take 43 to 67 minutes apiece, worked at $22-$34 an hour loaded at 1.496 times wages [BLS], and a build removes 38-47 percent of that effort, the hours saved are worth roughly $8,900 to $30,200 a year against an $8,000-to-$20,000 build — but payback still runs 4 to 28 months, and on the slower reading the three-year present value can land slightly negative. Observed: the peer table shows Cedar Valley's own front door already passes 4 of 6 checks, ahead of 5 of the 7 peers measured. Assumed, verify on the call: actual enquiry volume, minutes handled per enquiry, and whether a comparably capable intake already exists.

2-4 weeks · $8,000-$20,000 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the aggressive reading, returns $8,874-$30,213 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 4-28 months

### Lead recommendation

Open with the quote assembler — priced at $600 to $2,500, delivered in one to two weeks, and paying back inside the first one to two months on the target reading — because it is the smallest thing that produces something the owner can check before any bigger conversation starts. The diagnostic and the front-door build are worth raising only once that first piece is running and trusted. Once something is delivered, a founding-client care plan at $500 to $1,500 a month, locked for twelve months, keeps it maintained as volumes shift.

## Where they stand

The peer comparison argues for a specific order of operations. Cedar Valley sits behind on capital deployed — about $150,000 once the required matching money is counted, with 7 of the 11 comparable food and beverage grant recipients ahead of them — which the diagnostic in approach 2 is built to turn into a concrete next-investment number rather than a comparison. On front door quality, though, they already sit ahead of most of the group, passing 4 of 6 checks against only 2 of 7 peers doing better, so approach 3 closes a gap that barely exists and belongs third, not first.

On named competitors, no competitor is named on their site or in coverage of them [block10_competitors.named_by_them], so there is no rival to benchmark against directly. The only adjacent count on file is hiring: Cedar Valley shows no open roles on their careers page when read, and against the group they are not the one of 1 advertising openly — the entire hiring signal in this peer set is a single company, which tells me this dimension is too thin to read as an industry pattern either way.

On the wider economy: manufacturing employment nationally fell 1.8 percent between September 2023 and August 2026, a shrinking labour pool for these roles industry-wide, while total private compensation costs were climbing at 3.3 percent a year as of April 2026 — together suggesting the manual hours this plant pays for today will keep getting more expensive, not less.

## Technical read

The only named technology signals on file — a custom or unrecognized site platform, Google Analytics, and HubSpot [block6_tech_stack] — sit behind a web address that itself describes a healthcare patient-payments company [block1_what_they_make.self_description], not a pita chip plant, so none of it can be trusted as Cedar Valley's own stack until the real site is confirmed on the call. What can be trusted is the grant record: it names automation, quality/food-safety implementation and "map processing" as the funded scope [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description], implying some combination of line sensors, a QA logging step, or a scheduling tool already exists in some form, though the specific equipment was never recorded. The integration surface for any of the three builds — the order log, the machine data source, the enquiry inbox — is unknown and needs naming before a scope is fixed.

## Discovery questions

What is Cedar Valley's actual website and inbox, since the source on file resolves to an unrelated company? How many quotes go out in a typical month, and are they built from a spreadsheet, paper, or memory today? What machines and lines run the pita chip process, and do any already log shift time or scrap anywhere? What did the 2023 $75,000 automation award actually purchase, and is it fully installed and in use? What was the 2025 youth employment award used for, and is that hire still on staff? Roughly how many people work at the plant, and who currently owns quoting, quality logging, and inbound customer enquiries? How many wholesale, broker or retail enquiries arrive monthly, and how are they routed today?

artifacts.body:
Dear owner or president of Cedar Valley Selections Inc.,

The National Research Council's public record of your Industrial Research Assistance Program award — agreement title "Scale-Up Process and Implementation of Automation," filed in 2023 — describes your project in your own words as scale-up automation, quality assurance and food safety implementations, and map processing to increase efficiency, quality, and production capacity of your pita chip manufacturing facility, and carries a contribution of $75,000 (block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[1]).

That commitment tells me capital is already at work on your floor, which is exactly where idle time becomes a real cost rather than a theoretical one.

If the funded equipment runs somewhere between 5 and 15 percent below its available hours in a given year, the recoverable value of that idle time — measured as a share of the annual capital charge on the $75,000 already committed — sits somewhere between $375 and $1,250 CAD a year.

I would rather you correct that figure than trust it, because it rests entirely on a utilisation rate only you can see.

That is the fragment I cannot fill in from the outside: I have no visibility into how many hours your automation runs against how many it could, and the number above moves sharply depending on that answer.

We work with small food manufacturers to build a simple utilisation record — one page, updated weekly — so that number stops being invisible.

If the arithmetic above is wrong, telling us so is the whole point of this letter; a corrected figure is more useful to both of us than a polite non-reply.

We are offering early clients a founding-client rate, locked 12 months.

Sincerely,

—
Udaay Sikder
Nahl Technologies Inc.
Written under CASL; posted, not emailed.

figure.basis: no volume and no headcount, so the arithmetic is about the $75,000 of capital their award records rather than about hours
figure.means: the value of the funded equipment's IDLE TIME that a utilisation record would recover in a year. It is a share of the annual capital charge on the money they have already committed. It is NOT interest, NOT a financing cost, NOT a carrying cost, and NOT revenue. What it attacks: idle time on capital already committed

artifacts.body:
## The business

Cedar Valley Selections Inc. runs a pita chip manufacturing plant in Oldcastle. The IRAP grant record describes their own scope in their own words: scaling up automation, implementing quality assurance and food safety systems, and processing product through packaging — "map processing," which most plausibly reads as modified atmosphere packaging, standard for extending shelf life on a snack line, though that's worth confirming on the call rather than assumed further. The stated goal is efficiency, quality and production capacity at a single facility [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description]. That reads as a single-plant snack food operation moving from a largely manual process toward automated, QA-instrumented production, with work flowing from mixing and frying through seasoning, packaging and shipping. The 2023 IRAP award of $75,000, titled "Scale-Up Process and Implementation of Automation" [block2_grant_funded.agreement_title], funded that transition directly. A second, smaller 2025 IRAP Youth Employment award of $30,000 [block2_grant_funded.grant_awards[0]] suggests a junior technical or operations hire was brought on to run or extend that work — likely the person, alongside ownership, who actually touches the equipment day to day.

## Findings

1. The grant-funded automation has no utilization record attached to it. The 2023 award named "Scale-Up Process and Implementation of Automation" committed $75,000 of capital [block2_grant_funded.grant_amount], but nothing in the record says how much of that equipment's available time is actually being used today. If a working life of 5 to 10 years is assumed for equipment bought under this kind of contribution, and the asset is running somewhere between 45 and 70 percent of its available time — the figure we'd be asking Cedar Valley to correct — then, on a conservative reading, every point of idle time is worth $375 to $1,250 a year in recoverable capacity that a simple utilization log would surface.

2. Quality assurance and food safety tracking likely still runs on paper or spreadsheet. The agreement explicitly names QA and food-safety implementation as part of the funded scope [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description], which tells me this was being done by hand before the grant and may still be recorded by hand now. On a conservative reading, if the line runs somewhere between 120 and 500 machine-shifts a month, each carrying 8 to 25 minutes of manual recording at a wage of $22 to $34 loaded up 1.496 times by the manufacturing compensation multiplier the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes, that manual effort costs $6,300 to $34,300 a year fully loaded — money spent writing numbers down rather than making chips.

3. Inbound enquiries likely land on the same small team that runs production. With no open roles found on their careers page [block3_hiring_signals.open_roles_found] and no competitor named on their site or in coverage of them [block10_competitors.named_by_them], that suggests a small, owner-close team handling everything, including wholesale and buyer contact. If 10 to 60 enquiries a month each take 20 to 90 minutes at the same $22 to $34 wage, the conservative reading puts that at $1,316 to $11,755 a year spent just handling contact before anything is quoted.

## Three approaches

### 1. Utilization record

A first number about the funded equipment they can check themselves.

What gets built is a utilization record for the grant-funded automation line, drawn from whatever the equipment already logs — no new sensors, no new software purchase, just capturing and reporting what exists. It connects directly to the machinery funded under the 2023 award and returns one number Cedar Valley can check: how many hours out of its available time that equipment actually ran last month.

On the conservative reading, if the $75,000 of capital committed under that award [block2_grant_funded.grant_amount] is set against a working life of 5 to 10 years assumed for equipment bought this way, and the asset runs somewhere between 45 and 70 percent of its available time today, then a record that recovers 5 to 15 percent of that available time is worth $31 to $104 a month, or $375 to $1,250 a year. Against a $600 to $2,500 build, that pays back in month 6 at best and doesn't clear inside 36 months on the slow end — a modest number, because the point of this rung is the measurement itself, not the payback.

Feasibility, observed: the machines are the ones the 2023 grant named as funded scope [block2_grant_funded.agreement_title]. Assumed, verify on the call: what the equipment logs today, whether it's accessible without new hardware, and the real utilization percentage.

1-2 weeks · $600-$2,500 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the conservative reading, returns $375-$1,250 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 6-36 months

### 2. Machine data diagnostic

A measured answer to what QA tracking is actually costing on the floor.

What gets built is a weekly utilization and scrap report pulled from what the production line already records, aimed squarely at the manual quality and food-safety tracking the grant explicitly funded [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description]. It replaces however scrap, machine-shifts and QA checks are currently written down with a standing report someone reads instead of compiles.

On the target reading, if the line runs somewhere between 247 and 373 machine-shifts a month, each carrying 13.7 to 19.3 minutes of manual recording, done by someone earning $22 to $34 an hour loaded up 1.496 times by the manufacturing compensation multiplier the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes, that manual effort costs $22,190 to $73,425 a year fully loaded. A build removing 53 to 62 percent of that effort gives back 30 to 74 hours a month, worth $11,835 to $45,279 a year. Against a $2,500 to $8,000 diagnostic, that pays back somewhere between month 1 and month 9.

Feasibility, observed: the grant record names QA and food-safety implementation as funded scope. Assumed, verify on the call: actual machine-shift volume, the current recording method, and whether scrap data already exists anywhere machine-readable.

1-2 weeks · $2,500-$8,000 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the target reading, returns $11,834-$45,278 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 1-9 months

### 3. Enquiry front door

An intake that answers a buyer or wholesaler the hour they reach out.

What gets built is a front door that answers, captures and routes an enquiry the hour it lands — a different problem from the production floor, aimed at whoever currently fields wholesale, retail-buyer or ingredient-sourcing contact by hand.

On the target reading, if 27 to 43 enquiries arrive a month, each taking 43 to 67 minutes of staff time at $22 to $34 an hour loaded the same 1.496 times, that manual handling costs $7,606 to $29,388 a year fully loaded. A build removing 38 to 47 percent of that effort gives back 7 to 22 hours a month, worth $2,916 to $13,714 a year. Against an $8,000 to $20,000 build, that pays back in month 7 at best and doesn't clear inside 36 months at worst.

Feasibility, observed: the front door on file passes 4 of 6 checks and has a working contact form and mobile support, per the peer comparison. Assumed, verify on the call: whether that record actually reflects Cedar Valley Selections' own site — we hold no phone number or address for them, and the content read doesn't obviously describe a food manufacturer — and how enquiries are handled today.

2-4 weeks · $8,000-$20,000 CAD (founding-client rate, locked 12 months) · on the target reading, returns $2,915-$13,714 a year if the assumptions above hold · pays back in 7-36 months

### Lead recommendation

Open with the utilization record. At $600 to $2,500 it's small enough to say yes to on this call, it turns the grant's own equipment into the first number Cedar Valley can check and correct, and it sets up the diagnostic and the enquiry build as the next two rungs once that number is confirmed. Once anything is delivered, the care plan — $500 to $1,500 CAD a month, founding-client rate, locked 12 months — keeps it watched and adjusted as the operation changes.

## Where they stand

Commercially, the peer comparison points at two things. First, on capital deployed, Cedar Valley has committed about $150,000 once the required matching money is counted, and 7 of the 11 comparable food and beverage grant recipients we hold have deployed more than that — given the caveat that this group is too small at comparable size to say anything firm, read that as a difference in industry practice rather than a difference in scale, and a reason not to lead on capital appetite. Second, on the front door, they pass 4 of 6 checks against the record we hold, and only 2 of the 7 peers we could measure are ahead of them — that's the gap the enquiry-front-door approach is built to close, assuming the site record on file is actually theirs.

On named rivals: no competitor is named on their site or in coverage of them [block10_competitors.named_by_them]. Certifications show the same pattern — none published by Cedar Valley, and none published by any of the 7 peers we could measure — which tells me formal certification isn't how this peer set signals food safety, so the QA work the grant funded is more likely operational than certification-driven.

On the wider economy: All Employees, Manufacturing fell 1.8 percent between 2023-09-01 and 2026-08-01, the same count read straight from the agency that publishes it, which tells me manufacturing headcount nationally has been shrinking over the window this grant covers — a reason automating existing hours matters more than adding people. The Employment Cost Index for total compensation in private industry was running at a 3.3 percent twelve-month rate as of 2026-04-01, which is the pace wage bills are climbing at regardless of what Cedar Valley does next.

## Technical read

The only systems visibly on record are Google Analytics and HubSpot embeds and a custom or unrecognised site platform [block6_tech_stack.site_platform], attributed to a site that reads, in its own text, as a healthcare payments company rather than a pita chip manufacturer — that's a real inconsistency in the file, not a detail to build on, and it needs resolving on the call before any web-facing approach is scoped against it. On the production side, nothing is recorded directly; what's likely run — PLCs or an HMI on the automated line, a packaging system tied to the "map processing" scope, and QA data kept on paper or spreadsheet — is inferred from the grant description alone [block2_grant_funded.agreement_description], not observed. The integration surface for a utilization or scrap report depends entirely on what that equipment already logs, which is unknown. Architecture unknowns to raise directly: whether any data historian, SCADA or MES exists at all, and what, if anything, currently holds QA records in a form software could read.

## Discovery questions

What percentage of its available time does the automated line actually run today, and where would that be logged if we asked for it? How many machine-shifts run in a typical month, and how many minutes does QA or scrap recording take per shift? Who does that recording now, and is it the person hired under the 2025 Youth Employment award? Is there any system — spreadsheet, PLC log, paper form — that already captures utilization or scrap data? How many wholesale, retail-buyer or sourcing enquiries come in a month, and who answers them today? Is cedar.com actually Cedar Valley Selections' site, or is there a separate one we haven't seen? Does the company hold any food safety certification not published anywhere public? And what appetite is there for matching further capital the way the two IRAP awards required?
